nameStory: This jumping spider earned both its 'golden' and 'emerald' common names from its stunning metallic coloration that can shift between brilliant green and golden hues depending on the light. The scientific name 'aurantius' actually means 'golden' in Latin, though many specimens appear more emerald than gold. It's like having a tiny jewel with legs hopping around your garden!
description: The Golden Jumping Spider is one of the larger and most eye-catching jumping spiders you'll encounter in New England. These compact, robust spiders display gorgeous metallic green or black coloration with distinctive white racing stripes along their head and a white border crowning their abdomen. They're solitary hunters that don't build webs to catch prey, instead relying on their excellent vision and impressive jumping ability to pounce on unsuspecting insects. For a jumping spider, they're quite substantial in size and easy to spot when they're active.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Look for bright white side stripes running along each side of the head like racing stripes, plus a distinctive white border around the top edge of the abdomen that looks like a crown or headband

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact and robust with a chunky, rectangular build that's noticeably larger and more substantial than most other jumping spiders you'll see

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: A central line of fine hairs runs down the middle of the body, flanked by small white dots and thin lines that create a subtle striped pattern

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large, forward-facing eyes arranged in a row across the front of the head, giving them an almost cartoon-like appearance and excellent forward vision

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky motions with impressive jumps, often turning to look directly at you with their big front eyes when they notice your presence

habitat: Golden Jumping Spiders prefer sunny, open areas where they can hunt actively during the day. Look for them on wooden fences, deck railings, tree bark, and garden structures where they patrol for prey. They're particularly fond of areas with good sun exposure and plenty of flying insects to hunt.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge and become active as temperatures warm, beginning their hunting season on sunny days when flying insects are abundant.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible and active hunters. This is the best time to spot their metallic colors gleaming in bright sunlight.
seasonality.fall: Mating occurs and egg sacs are produced. Adults may still be seen on warm, sunny autumn days but become less active as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off, with the species overwintering as eggs or young spiderlings in protected locations under bark or in crevices.

funFact: Golden Jumping Spiders have color vision that's actually better than ours in some ways - they can see into the ultraviolet spectrum, which means the world looks completely different to them than it does to us, with hidden patterns and colors we can't even imagine!
confusionNotes: The metallic green coloration might remind you of some beetles or other insects, but remember that jumping spiders have eight legs and those distinctive big forward-facing eyes. Memory trick: 'Eight legs, eight eyes, but only four face forward to spy!'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called both 'golden' and 'emerald' jumping spiders, individual specimens tend to be more consistently one color or the other rather than changing colors. The dual common names reflect the natural variation in the population rather than color-changing ability.
compareHints: Since this is the only Paraphidippus species in New England, compare it to other large jumping spiders in the region. Most other jumping spiders lack the distinctive white racing stripes on the head and the metallic green or golden coloration. The combination of larger size, metallic sheen, and bold white markings makes Golden Jumping Spiders quite distinctive among the jumping spider family.
